strengths: Originality/significance: The paper explores a worthwhile direction—using reinforcement learning to construct complete integer solutions rather than merely supplying partial assignments to a conventional MILP solver. The two-phase feasibility/quality formulation and Transformer-GNN policy are potentially useful ideas.

Presentation: The overall pipeline, graph representation, action space, and search procedure are explained clearly, with helpful figures and pseudocode. The manuscript is generally readable and candidly acknowledges the restrictions to integer-only problems and local search.

Soundness: The method attains feasibility on all 100 reported test instances at each of the two tested sizes, and the architecture comparison and component ablations provide some evidence that the full model improves solution quality on this synthetic distribution.
Ethics/limitations: The application poses no evident material ethical risk, and the discussion honestly identifies limited global-search ability and lack of continuous-variable support.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not adequately supported. Evaluation uses only one highly restricted synthetic generator at two fixed sizes, with nonnegative constraint coefficients, nonnegative variables, and right-hand sides constructed to guarantee feasibility. In this setting, x=0 is always feasible and decreasing variables improves every Ax<=b constraint, making feasibility unusually easy and poorly representative of general MILPs.

Calling the method an end-to-end ML solver that eliminates reliance on traditional solvers is misleading: Algorithm 1 requires solving the LP relaxation to initialize x0 and obtain objr. The implementation and cost of that optimization are not specified or included in the comparison.

The claim of near-optimality on D100x50 is unsupported. RP Gap is measured against the best solution observed among the compared methods, not a certified optimum or bound. Thus a 1.33% RP Gap does not establish a 1.33% optimality gap. Likewise, the manuscript asserts optimality on D9x18 without reporting certificates.

The comparison is too weak for the claimed significance: it includes only Gurobi and two neural architecture variants, omitting basic local-search, rounding/repair, feasibility-pump, RL, and learning-based primal-heuristic baselines. Because all methods receive 100 seconds while training cost is unreported, computational efficiency is also unclear.

Results are reported only as averages over 100 instances, with no seeds, repeated training runs, variance, confidence intervals, failure distributions, or training/inference compute. Generalization across sizes, coefficient distributions, constraint senses, sparsities, and standard benchmark families is not tested.

Several technical details are ambiguous or problematic. Equation 7 uses obj_t although the reward should apparently depend on the post-action state; the claim that delta_b lies in [0,1] is false in general; division by |obj_b| is undefined when obj_b=0; and the phase-one summed-slack reward can reward improving already satisfied constraints rather than specifically repairing violations.

The Actor-Critic specification is insufficiently rigorous. The text describes Q(S,A), but the depicted critic appears not to consume actions and may instead estimate V(S). The factorization of the exponentially large joint action, temporal-return target, discounting, exploration, losses, and update equations are not given.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the paper omits model dimensions, number of layers/heads, local-region size Delta, learning rate, optimizer settings, discount factor, rollout length, stopping thresholds, initialization/rounding rule, hardware, training time, number of training instances, and random seeds. No code or complete instance-generation implementation is provided.

The architecture concatenates A^T into each variable token, tying feature dimensionality to the number of constraints and raising scalability and cross-size generalization concerns. Full self-attention over variables is quadratic, yet memory/runtime scaling is not evaluated.

Overall, the idea is promising and the paper is readable, but the overly easy synthetic setting, absence of certified optimality evidence and meaningful baselines, methodological ambiguities, and severe reproducibility gaps prevent the evidence from substantiating the broad solver claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: producing complete feasible integer solutions without requiring supervised solution labels or delegating a residual integer subproblem to a solver.

The proposed combination of bipartite message passing, global Transformer attention, and phase-specific actor/critic heads is coherent, and the two-phase distinction between feasibility search and objective improvement is intuitively motivated.
The method is described with useful equations, diagrams, and pseudocode. The component ablation in Table 3 covers periodic embeddings, the phase token, and separate phase-specific layers.

The authors appropriately acknowledge that local search cannot guarantee global optimality and that the current method does not handle continuous variables. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: the synthetic evaluation distribution is exceptionally easy and structurally biased. In Table 1 of the manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/cdc1dae8ca6c4a4790211bf58ed5b8e4/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}, A has only positive entries, b=Aξ+ε is positive, and variables have lower bound zero. Consequently, x=0 is a known feasible solution to every generated instance. The reported 100% feasibility and sub-0.1-second first-feasible times therefore provide little evidence that the method can resolve difficult feasibility structures.

Soundness and significance: evaluation is limited to two synthetic distributions, with at most 100 variables and 50 constraints. These instances are trivial for Gurobi, which solves them in under one second, yet every method is given 100 seconds. There are no standard MILP benchmarks, real applications, distribution shifts, larger instances, or problems with mixed-sign coefficients, equality constraints in their native form, finite/general bounds, or continuous variables.

The title and conclusions repeatedly present a general MILP solver, but all experimental variables are non-binary integers; this is a pure integer linear-program subclass rather than general MILP. Moreover, inference obtains an LP-relaxation solution and lower bound, apparently using a conventional optimizer, which substantially qualifies the claims of operating “solely on ML” and eliminating reliance on traditional solvers.

The experimental comparison is inadequate. Beyond Gurobi, the only baselines are weaker neural architecture variants of the authors' own method. There is no comparison with simple constructive heuristics, local search from the rounded LP solution, feasibility pump, SCIP, random/greedy policies, the cited RL feasibility method, or modern learning-based primal heuristics. Thus the results do not establish that reinforcement learning itself provides value.

The phase-1 reward sums changes in signed constraint slack rather than directly measuring the number or magnitude of violations. It can reward increasing slack in already satisfied constraints without repairing violated ones. On the chosen positive packing instances, simply decreasing variables toward the trivially feasible origin naturally maximizes this signal, making the claimed learning of general variable–constraint relationships unconvincing.

The “relative primal gap” is measured against the best solution found among compared methods rather than a certified optimum, and only aggregate means are reported. There are no per-instance distributions, variances, confidence intervals, multiple random seeds, optimality certificates, or statistical tests. The small differences between neural variants therefore cannot support the architectural conclusions.

Reproducibility is poor: the manuscript omits essential architecture dimensions, number of layers/heads, local-region size Δ, learning rate and optimizer settings, discounting and entropy choices, exact actor–critic losses, rollout and termination limits, inference action rule, hardware, training time, and random seeds. No code or generated datasets are provided.

Originality is limited to a particular assembly of established actor–critic learning, bipartite GNNs, Transformers, periodic embeddings, and local search. The potentially interesting two-phase reward design is not validated on sufficiently challenging data, while the claim of being the first ML method to incrementally find better complete feasible solutions is too broad given the narrow related-work comparison.

Presentation is generally readable, but important algorithmic details remain ambiguous, including whether reward equations use the pre-action or post-action state, how the joint action over all variables is factorized, and how the critic represents Q(S,A). These omissions prevent the methodology from being independently reconstructed. Overall, the central general-solver claims are not supported by the evidence, warranting rejection rather than a borderline rating.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper targets an important problem—learning to construct complete integer solutions rather than merely fixing variables for a conventional MILP solver. The combination of a two-phase RL objective, local search, bipartite GCN, and global Transformer is a potentially useful research direction.

Soundness: The method explicitly checks feasibility, separates feasibility discovery from objective improvement, evaluates 100 held-out instances per dataset, and includes a reasonably informative factorial ablation of periodic embeddings, phase tokens, and phase-specific heads.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally readable and well organized. The diagrams, equations, and pseudocode communicate the main search process and architecture clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/d4e17bea5f4b4f93a5cd7e5f14a37146/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Limitations/ethics: The authors appropriately acknowledge the restriction to integer-only problems and the inability of local search to guarantee global optimality. The work uses synthetic optimization instances and raises no apparent human-subject, privacy, or other material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The instance generator produces an unusually easy and narrow packing family: A has only positive entries, b=Aξ+ε is positive, and every variable has lower bound zero. Consequently, x=0 is always an immediately available feasible solution. This substantially weakens the 100% feasible-rate and sub-second first-feasible-solution results and does not support claims about general MILPs with mixed-sign coefficients, covering/equality constraints, finite or negative bounds, or heterogeneous variable types.

Soundness/significance: Evaluation covers only two fixed-size synthetic distributions (9×18 and 100×50). There are no standard MILP benchmarks, real applications, distribution shifts, size generalization tests, trivial/random local-search controls, feasibility-pump comparisons, or competitive learned-search baselines. Comparing primarily against Gurobi and weaker versions of the authors' own architecture cannot isolate the benefit of learned guidance.

Soundness: “Optimal” and “near-optimal” are not adequately established. Relative Primal Gap is measured against the best incumbent found among the compared methods, rather than a certified optimum or solver bound. Therefore a 1.33% RP Gap does not demonstrate proximity to the true optimum, and even the 0% result on the small dataset only demonstrates matching the best tested incumbent unless optimality certificates are reported.

Soundness/presentation: Important algorithmic details are ambiguous or inconsistent. The text defines a critic Q(S,A), but Figure 6 appears to feed it state features without the action; the reward equations alternate between t and t+1 quantities; and the assertion that δb lies in [0,1] is not generally guaranteed. The factorization of the exponentially large joint action over variables and the precise actor-critic loss are also unspecified.

Reproducibility: Essential details are absent, including optimizer and LP-relaxation implementation, local-region size Δ, training episode and rollout lengths, stopping thresholds, learning rate, discount and entropy coefficients, network widths/depths/heads, action sampling policy, random seeds, hardware, parameter counts, training time, and uncertainty across independent runs. No code or complete configuration is provided.

Originality/generalizability: Concatenating c with A^T into each variable token makes the representation dimension depend on the number of constraints and appears sensitive to constraint ordering. The paper does not explain tensor shapes, permutation handling, or how one trained model could process varying numbers of constraints, which limits the claimed graph-based generality.

The claim of an approach based “solely on ML” or eliminating reliance on traditional solvers is overstated because every inference run begins by solving an LP relaxation to obtain x0 and a lower bound. The computational cost and software used for this step are not included in the analysis.

Although the manuscript honestly notes integer-only variables and local-search limitations, it does not adequately discuss the much more decisive limitations of the highly structured generator, lack of optimality certificates, fixed input sizes, missing runtime accounting, and absence of variability estimates. These evidential and reproducibility weaknesses prevent acceptance despite the promising idea.

strengths: The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear, with useful diagrams, equations, and pseudocode explaining the two-phase search procedure. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/bd809506a1a14fae8c1fa4fbe02d1c87/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed combination of actor-critic learning, feasibility-aware rewards, local search, and a message-passing/Transformer architecture is an interesting direction for learned integer-programming heuristics. Avoiding labeled optimal solutions is also attractive.
The evaluation includes 100 test instances at each of four sizes, component ablations, several reward-bias settings, and an investigation of neighborhood size.

The appendix reports the synthetic-data generator, hardware, software versions, optimizer settings, and high-level training configuration. No immediate research-ethics concern is apparent for these synthetic optimization experiments.
weaknesses: The central soundness issue is unresolved integrality. Algorithm 1 initializes x0 with the LP-relaxation solution, while every subsequent action changes each coordinate by an integer. Any fractional part of x0 is therefore invariant, so a generic fractional LP solution can never become integer-feasible. Moreover, the feasibility vector f and rewards check linear constraints and bounds but not integrality. No rounding or integer projection is specified. Consequently, the reported 100% feasible rates and the claim of producing complete integer solutions are not supported as written.

The benchmark is an exceptionally narrow and easy packing-style family rather than representative MILP: every variable is integer, A has nonnegative coefficients, bounds are [0,infinity), and b=Aξ+ε with positive ξ and ε. Thus x=0 is a known feasible solution for every instance, making first-feasible-solution time largely uninformative. The experiments cover neither genuinely mixed continuous/integer problems nor varied signs, equality constraints, difficult feasibility, or established MILP benchmarks.

The method is not actually independent of traditional optimization machinery in the stated sense. Algorithm 1 requires solving an LP relaxation to obtain both x0 and objr, and the implementation lists Gurobi. This materially qualifies the repeated claims of a full end-to-end solver operating without reliance on off-the-shelf solvers.

The empirical comparison does not establish practical significance. Gurobi already obtains 100% feasibility in less than one second and gaps of only 0.00–0.03%, outperforming the learned method on solution quality. Its timing is reported only as '<1s' because of logging resolution, preventing a meaningful first-solution comparison. Training cost is omitted, and no objective-versus-time or equal-quality runtime analysis is presented.

The baselines are insufficient. Local search is initialized using the proposed agent's phase-1 output, while the MLP/CNN variants are only internal architectural substitutions. There is no comparison with established feasibility-pump, learned primal-heuristic, or other modern integer-search methods on a shared benchmark; the claim that existing approaches cannot be compared is too broad.

The evaluation uses only same-distribution synthetic instances, apparently with size-specific training. It reports no random-seed variation, confidence intervals, statistical tests, training stability, out-of-distribution generalization, or scaling beyond 300 variables. Claims about general MILP-solving capability and long-range reasoning therefore exceed the evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the appendix. The authors do not provide their implementation, trained models, seeds, or generated test instances, and omit crucial hyperparameters such as discount factor, episode limits, warm-up/grace periods, local-region size, complete Transformer configuration, action factorization, and model-selection procedure.

Algorithm 2 appears internally inconsistent: when a candidate is rejected, it resets xt+1 to xb without recomputing ft+1 and objt+1, yet returns the entire state St+1. The actor-critic update also does not specify whether the TD advantage is detached or how the joint action probability over all variables is constructed.

The claimed theoretical foundation is weak. Proposition 1 is merely the standard fact that an LP relaxation supplies a lower bound; it neither justifies the reward design nor provides convergence, feasibility, or approximation guarantees. The assertion that results 'support Proposition 1' is misplaced because the proposition holds independently of those experiments.

Presentation is readable, but central terminology is overstated: 'optimal' is inferred from equality with a finite-time best-known solution rather than an explicitly reported optimality certificate, and 'MILP solver' is used although the experiments treat only pure-integer instances. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations discussion covering this restricted generator, LP-solver dependence, absent guarantees, quadratic attention costs, and amortized training expense. Ethical risk is low, but total training compute and environmental cost are not reported.

strengths: Presentation: The paper is generally readable and well organized, with useful diagrams, equations, pseudocode, and a clear explanation of the two-phase feasibility/optimization strategy.

Originality: Treating complete integer assignments as an RL-guided local-search process is a potentially interesting direction, particularly compared with learned heuristics that predict only partial assignments.

Soundness-positive: The evaluation reports feasibility rate, time to first feasible solution, and objective gap across several problem sizes. The inclusion of architecture ablations and neighborhood-size experiments is useful.

Significance-positive: A learned heuristic that reliably produces feasible non-binary integer solutions without requiring a downstream MILP completion step could be valuable if demonstrated on realistic, diverse benchmarks.
weaknesses: Soundness: The algorithm is not valid as written. Algorithm 1 initializes x0 with the LP-relaxation solution, while every action changes a variable by an integer amount. A generic LP solution is fractional, so its fractional parts remain invariant and the trajectory can never satisfy the integrality constraints. No rounding or other integrality-restoration operation is specified, and the feasibility reward accounts only for linear constraints and bounds. This omission directly undermines the central claim that the method produces integer-feasible solutions.

Soundness: The claimed independence from traditional solvers is misleading. Every episode calls Relaxation(M) and requires an optimal LP solution and lower bound; the experimental environment lists Gurobi, but the implementation and cost of this operation are not reported. The method is therefore neither fully solver-independent nor fully end-to-end in the stated sense.

Soundness: The evaluation distribution is extremely narrow and favorable. All variables are nonnegative integers, all nonzero constraint coefficients are positive, objective coefficients are nonpositive, and right-hand sides are generated from a planted positive vector. This is a synthetic pure-integer packing family—not general MILP—and zero is always an immediately available feasible solution. Results on this family do not support claims about mixed-integer programs, arbitrary coefficient signs, continuous variables, equality constraints, or realistic feasibility difficulty.

Soundness and significance: Gurobi is already faster and more accurate on every reported size: it solves all instances in under one second and obtains gaps of 0.00–0.03%, whereas the proposed method is allowed 100 seconds and obtains roughly 0.34–0.47% on larger instances. Reporting only first-feasible time for the learned method obscures this comparison; time-to-quality curves and equal-budget results are needed.

Evaluation: The baselines are inadequate. Local search is given the proposed method's feasible output, the neural baselines differ mainly in architecture, and relevant learned primal heuristics are dismissed rather than adapted or evaluated. There are no comparisons with standard MILP primal heuristics, feasibility pump variants, open-source solvers, or simple rounding-and-repair baselines.

Evaluation: The paper uses only 100 generated test instances per size, reports no confidence intervals or variation over training seeds, and does not test standard collections such as MIPLIB, distinct MILP families, distribution shift, or cross-size generalization. Matching a best-known value is also described as reaching the optimum without consistently reporting an optimality certificate.

Technical specification: Several legitimate inputs make the reward undefined, including objr=0 in delta_t,r and objr=objb in delta_t,b. Algorithm 2 also references xb before a first feasible solution necessarily exists and can overwrite x without explicitly recomputing the associated feasibility and objective components of the returned state. These edge cases are material for a purported general solver.

Originality: Most ingredients—actor-critic learning, bipartite MILP graphs, MPNNs, global-attention graph encoders, reward shaping, and local search—are established. Proposition 1 is the elementary LP-relaxation lower-bound inequality, not a substantive theoretical foundation. The paper does not provide convergence, feasibility, or approximation guarantees.

Reproducibility: Hyperparameters and source repositories for borrowed components are listed, but the paper provides no implementation release, generated instances, random seeds, complete model configuration, training time, inference-step limits, relaxation procedure, rounding rule, or precise policy factorization. The central experimental results cannot be reliably reconstructed from the manuscript.

Presentation and limitations: The prose and figures are clear, but broad terms such as “MILP solver,” “full end-to-end,” “without reliance on off-the-shelf solvers,” and “near-optimal” overstate the evidence. There is no dedicated limitations discussion acknowledging the restricted packing distribution, reliance on LP relaxation, absence of guarantees, or weak scalability evidence (only up to 300 variables and 100 constraints).

Ethics: No acute human-subject or data-privacy concern is apparent because the experiments use synthetic optimization instances. Nevertheless, the paper does not discuss computational cost or possible risks of deploying an uncertified heuristic in consequential optimization settings. This is secondary to the technical concerns.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper explores a worthwhile direction—using reinforcement learning to construct and iteratively improve complete integer solutions instead of predicting only a partial assignment.

Soundness: The two-phase formulation separates feasibility discovery from objective improvement in an intuitive way, and the feasibility-based reward is directly tied to constraint and bound violations.

Evaluation: The authors test four problem sizes using 100 instances each and include architecture ablations, alternative neighborhood sizes, a local-search comparison, and feasibility-specific metrics.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized; its diagrams, equations, pseudocode, and appendix make the proposed workflow comparatively easy to follow.
Ethics: The work presents no evident material ethical or societal risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of a standalone solver that does not rely on traditional solvers is not established. Both training and inference begin with Relaxation(M), which supplies an optimal LP solution and bound, but the implementation and runtime cost of this optimization are not reported. If Gurobi or another LP solver performs this step, the claimed independence is misleading.

Soundness/significance: All experiments use a narrow synthetic family in which every variable is integer, A has only positive coefficients, variables have lower bound zero, and b is explicitly generated from a feasible integer vector. This excludes continuous variables, signed coefficients, finite upper bounds, equalities, and realistic structured instances, so it provides little evidence for the broad claims about general MILP solving or multiple combinatorial-optimization tasks.

Significance: Gurobi finds a feasible solution in under one second on every dataset and has a smaller reported gap than the learned method. The learned solver is allowed 100 seconds, yet the paper reports only time to its first feasible solution—not time-quality curves or time to its final solution. Consequently, no practical advantage over conventional optimization is demonstrated, and training cost is omitted.

Evaluation: Results are reported only on IID test instances from the training generator. It is unclear whether a separate model is trained for every dimension, and there are no tests of transfer across sizes, distribution shift, standard MILP benchmarks, or real applications.

Evaluation: There are no repeated-training runs, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. RL performance can vary substantially with initialization and sampling, so single aggregate numbers do not adequately support small gap differences such as 0.30% versus 0.31%.

Theory/originality: Proposition 1 is merely the standard LP-relaxation lower-bound property. It neither guarantees that the proposed reward shaping improves search nor supplies an optimality or convergence result; describing the learning and search strategies as theoretically grounded overstates its role.

Methodological detail: The actor-critic specification is incomplete, including the joint-action parameterization, inference-time action selection, discount factor, step limits, warm-up and grace periods, local-region size, and several network details. The reward also contains divisions by |obj_r| and |obj_r-obj_b| without handling zero denominators.

Reproducibility: The appendix identifies hardware, optimizer settings, and upstream components, but does not provide the paper's code, generated datasets or seeds, trained checkpoints, training duration, or enough hyperparameters to reconstruct the results reliably.

Limitations/presentation: The paper lacks a dedicated limitations discussion and does not acknowledge the synthetic generator's simplicity, dependence on LP relaxation, per-distribution training, absence of optimality guarantees, or potentially substantial training and inference costs. These omissions contribute to overbroad claims of achieving near-optimal solutions and laying groundwork for a unified solver.

strengths: The paper targets an important gap: producing feasible ILP solutions directly, including non-binary integer variables, rather than relying on a solver to repair learned predictions.

RL-SPH combines phase-specific rewards, structured variable selection, and a Transformer-based graph policy in a coherent start-heuristic framework. The ability to initialize from either an LP solution or a simple random assignment is practically appealing.

Experiments report 100% feasibility on the evaluated test sets, and the ablation in Table 3 provides useful evidence that the Transformer encoder is particularly important: configurations without it obtain 0% feasibility on combinatorial auction instances.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with diagrams, pseudocode, dataset-generation details, training times, and an explicit discussion of the suboptimality risk introduced when RL-SPH solutions are used to fix variables.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee is invalid. Proposition 1 argues that a strictly increasing violation sequence bounded above by zero must converge to zero and reach feasibility at a finite T. Bounded monotone convergence only implies convergence to some value at most zero; it neither makes the limit zero nor establishes finite-time attainment. Moreover, the paper never proves that the learned policy satisfies the proposition's assumptions. Consequently, claims that a well-trained agent is “guaranteed” to find a feasible solution and that the method has a theoretical foundation are unsupported. The comparison with classical heuristics does not establish equal computational budgets. Each SCIP heuristic runs until its own termination condition, while RL-SPH runs until all baselines finish; GPU inference is compared with solver heuristics without a clear wall-clock accounting. The stated primal integral is a sum over “timesteps,” but agent steps and solver events are not comparable, and the time discretization and common horizon are unspecified. For RL-SPH+SCIP, it is also unclear whether the five seconds used to generate fixing solutions are included in the 50-second limit.

The experimental scope is too narrow for the broad general-ILP claims. Four of five benchmarks contain only binary variables. Non-binary support is tested on one synthetic family with nonnegative constraints, a planted feasible point, and x=0 as an immediate feasible solution. There are no heterogeneous real-world MIPLIB-style instances, equality-heavy cases, mixed variable types, distribution shifts, or tests at unseen sizes.

Important comparisons are missing. In particular, Smart Feasibility Pump—the cited RL method from which the non-binary benchmark is drawn—is not evaluated. The isolated SCIP heuristics are run with presolving and branching disabled, which does not represent their normal operating context, while the solver-combination experiment covers only IS and the synthetic NBI dataset.

The headline “44× lower primal gap” and “2.3× lower primal integral” are not defined by an explicit aggregation formula and are difficult to reconcile with Table 1. Best-known solutions are defined retrospectively as the best result among compared methods, and PG/PI are averaged only over instances on which a method succeeds, making low-feasibility methods appear deceptively strong. The tables mix symmetric standard deviations with unexplained asymmetric error notation, and no multi-seed uncertainty or statistical tests are reported.

Several algorithmic details and edge cases are unresolved. Equations and Algorithm 3 divide by max(|c|), which can be zero; variable-selection probabilities can have a zero denominator when no eligible constraint exists; Eq. 7 appears to use “all variables violate bounds” where “any variable” is intended; and the factorization of the joint action policy, inference rule, discount factor, Transformer dimensions, and attention/masking construction are not fully specified.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite useful partial implementation details. The manuscript links upstream components and PAS code but provides no RL-SPH repository, evaluation scripts, generated instances, checkpoints, or random seeds. Results appear to come from a single training run, so the stability of the RL method cannot be assessed.

No material research-ethics concern is apparent, and the stated optimality limitation is appropriate. However, the flawed guarantee, incomparable timing protocol, and limited non-binary evidence are substantive soundness issues that prevent acceptance rather than limitations that can be addressed through wording alone.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: quickly obtaining feasible ILP solutions, including solutions with non-binary integer variables, without requiring labeled optimal solutions.

The proposed combination of reinforcement learning, variable-neighborhood search, and a Transformer-based graph model is plausible and reasonably clearly motivated. Algorithms, reward equations, dataset-generation details, hardware, training times, and several hyperparameters are provided.

The reported in-distribution results are promising: RL-SPH reaches 100% feasibility on the tested instances, and the ablation in Table 3 provides some evidence that the Transformer encoder and reward-context design matter.
The authors appropriately acknowledge that fixing variables in RL-SPH+SCIP can introduce suboptimality. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: the claimed theoretical feasibility guarantee is invalid. Proposition 1 assumes positive constraint improvement at every step, an assumption that training does not guarantee, and then incorrectly infers that a strictly increasing sequence bounded above by zero must reach zero at a finite T. For example, for the feasible ILP constraint -x <= -100 with x initially 0, incrementing x once gives positive constraint reward and respects the bounds, yet x at T=1 remains infeasible. More generally, monotone bounded convergence neither implies a zero limit nor finite-time attainment. Thus the conclusion's claim of a theoretical guarantee from an initially infeasible solution is unsupported.

Soundness/evaluation: the headline 44x primal-gap and 2.3x primal-integral improvements do not follow from a clearly fair protocol. Each classical heuristic runs until its own termination condition, whereas RL-SPH runs until all baselines finish, effectively giving it the maximum baseline runtime. Runtime distributions and a common wall-clock-budget comparison are not reported, despite RL-SPH also using an A100 GPU.

The primal-integral definition is ambiguous and appears inconsistent: PG is defined as a percentage through multiplication by 100, but an absent incumbent is assigned PG=1, and PI is written as an unweighted sum over unspecified timesteps rather than a wall-clock integral. The sampling interval and treatment of differing termination times are missing, making the central speed claim difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The evidence for general non-binary ILPs is particularly weak. NBI is omitted from the direct comparison with start heuristics and is tested only against SCIP in the combined-solver experiment. Its synthetic generator uses positive A, nonpositive minimization costs, nonnegative variables, and b=Aξ+ε; consequently, the all-zero vector is trivially feasible. This does not substantiate broad claims about learning feasibility for general integer programs.

The actor is described as using c, A, the current variable values, and a bound indicator, while constraint slacks f and the right-hand side b appear only in variable selection and the critic. Consequently, action choices do not directly observe violation magnitudes or RHS values. The manuscript does not explain how such a policy can robustly determine constraint-restoring directions across general signed and scaled ILPs.

Significance/generalization: all training and testing use matched synthetic generators at a single problem size. There are no established real-world benchmarks, heterogeneous public MILP collections, scale-shift tests, or out-of-distribution experiments. RL-SPH+SCIP is evaluated on only IS and the easy synthetic NBI family, rather than all five benchmarks.

Originality is plausible but not convincingly established. The main ingredients—actor-critic learning, learned feasibility-pump-style search, graph Transformers, and local neighborhoods—are established ideas. The cited Smart Feasibility Pump work, which also applies RL to integer-program feasibility, is not substantively distinguished or experimentally compared, weakening the claim that RL-SPH is the first method to explicitly learn feasibility.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims. The bespoke RL-SPH implementation is not released; external repositories cover only constituent modules or a baseline. Exact inference procedure, model dimensions, training seeds, number of independent training runs, stochastic-variance analysis, timing/synchronization details, and precise PI computation are absent. Only SCIP randomization is said to be fixed.

Presentation is generally readable, but consequential inconsistencies remain: Section 4 announces 'two experiments' and then lists three; Equation 7 appears to require every variable to violate its bounds where the prose intends any violation; Appendix E assigns both seed and neighboring counts to p despite Algorithm 3 using p and q; and several algorithmic edge cases, such as zero objective coefficients causing normalization by max|c|, are not addressed.

The limitations discussion is too narrow. It honestly notes possible suboptimality from variable fixing, but does not acknowledge the invalid guarantee, restricted synthetic distributions, trivial feasibility structure of NBI, compute asymmetry, lack of cross-distribution evidence, or incomplete reproducibility. These are central limitations rather than minor matters of reach.

strengths: The manuscript is clear and visually polished, with a coherent progression from the ILP formulation through the RL design, search algorithm, experiments, and appendices. Figures and pseudocode make the proposed method relatively easy to follow. RL-SPH addresses a useful and insufficiently explored problem: learning a start primal heuristic that can produce feasible solutions without delegating feasibility recovery entirely to an ILP solver. Its support for non-binary integer actions is also a meaningful extension beyond predominantly binary predict-and-search methods.

The empirical results are promising. RL-SPH attains 100% feasibility on all reported benchmarks; on the four direct start-heuristic comparisons, it frequently improves primal gap and primal integral substantially. The solver-combination experiment also suggests that its feasible solutions can usefully warm-start or reduce subsequent search.

The inclusion of random and LP initializations, architecture ablations, an ablation of the toward-optimal bias, training times, software versions, dataset sizes, and algorithmic pseudocode provides useful diagnostic evidence rather than only a headline comparison.
The paper acknowledges that aggressive variable fixing can sacrifice optimality. No sensitive data, human-subject research, or immediate material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central theoretical feasibility claim is unsupported. Proposition 1 argues that a strictly increasing sequence of aggregate negative slacks, merely because it is upper-bounded by zero, must reach zero at a finite time T. This is false without an additional minimum-progress, discreteness, or convergence assumption; a bounded monotone sequence can converge to a negative value or approach zero without attaining it. Moreover, the proposition assumes positive constraint reward and satisfied bounds at every step but does not establish that the learned policy ensures either condition. Thus statements that a well-trained agent is “guaranteed” to find feasibility and that the method has a “theoretical foundation” should be removed or substantially revised.

The evidence for general non-binary ILPs is too narrow for the paper’s broad claims. There is only one synthetic NBI family, and its construction has A>0, b=Aξ+ε>0, x≥0, so the all-zero integer vector is immediately feasible. Random initialization is not evaluated on NBI, and the direct comparison with start heuristics in Table 1 excludes NBI. Consequently, the experiments do not convincingly demonstrate difficult feasibility recovery for general integer-variable problems.

Runtime fairness and metric construction require clarification. RL-SPH is allowed to run until all baseline heuristics have terminated, rather than receiving the termination time of each comparator, and it uses a GPU while SCIP heuristics are principally CPU algorithms. The paper defines primal integral as a sum over timesteps but does not specify the wall-clock sampling/integration procedure. PG and PI are also averaged only over instances on which a method finds a feasible solution, which makes low-feasibility methods appear artificially strong unless feasibility is always considered jointly.

The evaluation appears to use a single trained model/run per dataset: reported deviations are across instances rather than independent training seeds, and there are no confidence intervals or paired significance tests. Generalization is assessed only on same-generator, same-scale test instances; there is no size, distribution, or real-world transfer evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript links component implementations and PAS but does not provide an RL-SPH repository or trained checkpoints. Important details remain underspecified, including action-logit construction, exact Transformer dimensions, inference limits, time accounting, the number of solutions used for unanimous fixing, and behavior when no unanimous value exists. Equation 7 also appears to use “all variables violate bounds” where the surrounding explanation suggests “any variable,” creating a consequential implementation ambiguity.

The limitations discussion is honest but too narrow: it focuses almost exclusively on suboptimality from variable fixing and does not address the invalid guarantee, restricted synthetic NBI setting, hardware dependence, lack of multi-seed analysis, or limited out-of-distribution evidence. Given these soundness and evidential gaps, the promising idea does not yet meet the reliability expected for acceptance.

strengths: Originality/significance: Framing learned feasibility repair as a standalone start primal heuristic is useful, particularly because feasible incumbents are prerequisites for many downstream ILP heuristics. The combination of a two-phase reward, feasibility-aware variable selection, and an ILP-oriented Transformer is a meaningful systems contribution.

Empirical scope: The paper compares against several SCIP heuristic families and three learned baselines, reports feasibility rate, first-solution time, primal gap, and primal integral, and includes ablations, distribution/size/density shifts, solver integration, and MIPLIB tests.

Evidence on the in-distribution benchmarks is promising: RL-SPH attains 100% feasibility on all five test sets and often improves solution quality or time-to-feasibility over methods that also attain 100% feasibility.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The main algorithm, reward cases, hyperparameters, hardware/software environment, dataset sizes, and baseline families are documented, and the limitations section candidly discusses computational bottlenecks, scale, nonlinear constraints, and limited optimality.
Research ethics concerns are limited for this methodological work; no human data are involved, and the paper does not make problematic claims about social deployment.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 1 does not establish the claimed theoretical reward-feasibility alignment of RL-SPH. It assumes that every phase-1 transition has positive aggregate constraint reward and no bound violation—the behavior that must itself be guaranteed. Reward maximization, especially with objective and exploration terms and restricted variable selection, does not imply these assumptions. Thus the proposition is essentially a conditional monotonic-progress statement, not a feasibility guarantee for the learned policy.

The proof additionally asserts a fixed positive minimum improvement merely because integer variables are discrete. This needs assumptions such as rational coefficients and an appropriate bounded/discrete reachable set; with arbitrary real coefficients and unbounded integer domains, the stated argument does not follow. The reported 95.2% empirical 'trajectory adherence' also lacks a precise denominator and does not repair the missing guarantee.

There is a major architecture/reproducibility inconsistency. Each selected variable apparently includes its full column of (c^T|A), which is projected to the hidden size; the dataset-dependent parameter counts support an input dimension tied to the number of constraints. Yet the same joint model is claimed to run on MIPLIB instances having 24 to 4,875 constraints and on heterogeneous variable domains. The paper does not explain padding, resizing, permutation handling, or any dimension-independent encoder, so the prominent MIPLIB generalization experiment cannot be reproduced from the described method.

The evidence for general non-binary ILP feasibility is weak. Four of the five principal benchmarks are binary, while the sole synthetic NBI family has A>0, b=Aξ+ε>0, x>=0, making x=0 trivially feasible; its sparse random initialization is also far inside the feasible region. This does not substantiate broad claims about repairing difficult non-binary ILPs with mixed-sign coefficients, equalities, finite bounds, or tightly coupled domains.

Evaluation fairness and uncertainty are insufficiently controlled. Learned methods use an A100 while SCIP heuristics use CPUs, but resource accounting is not normalized; termination horizons depend on when baselines finish; PG, PI, and FT are conditioned on successful instances; and results appear to use one trained model per dataset without variation across training seeds or paired significance tests. Mean±variation across instances does not quantify training instability.

The MIPLIB evaluation uses only 17 instances without a stated selection protocol, enabling selection bias, and includes continuous variables even though the formal problem and integrality argument assume all variables are integer. It is not explained how continuous variables are represented or updated. RL-SPH is also substantially worse than RHF on several listed cases, including scpk4, toll-like, rail507, and bppc8-02, making the broad unified-solver interpretation premature.

Reproducibility is only partial: important architectural dimensions and action-factorization details are deferred to unspecified 'same configuration' external code; dataset and training seeds, precise baseline resource usage, BKS construction, checkpoint-selection rules for RL-SPH, and executable code for the proposed method are not supplied. Several pseudocode state transitions are also implicit or undefined.

The limitations discussion is welcome but does not acknowledge the most consequential limitations: the conditional nature of the proposition, the trivial structure of the non-binary feasibility benchmark, and the apparent fixed-constraint-dimension architecture. The generic impact statement also overlooks risks from deploying approximate optimization decisions in consequential allocation settings, although this is not independently decisive.

strengths: Presentation/originality: The paper is clearly organized and proposes a coherent combination of actor–critic learning, feasibility-aware variable selection, and a Transformer-based policy. The two-phase repair-and-improvement design is intuitive and is described with equations, pseudocode, and useful ablations.

Empirical breadth: The evaluation includes five generated problem families, several classical and learned baselines, initialization variants, distribution/size/density shifts, solver integration, and limited MIPLIB tests. RL-SPH often finds better incumbents faster than SCIP's isolated rounding heuristics, so the learned search policy appears empirically promising.

Reproducibility: The appendix provides dataset-generation parameters, optimizer and architecture settings, hardware/software versions, baseline implementations, training times, and fairly detailed pseudocode. These details would facilitate reimplementation.

The paper acknowledges several genuine limitations, including quadratic variable-selection cost, degradation on very large or structurally unfamiliar instances, restricted unit-step actions, and the lack of nonlinear-constraint experiments. I found no unresolved material research-ethics concern, although the impact statement is generic.
weaknesses: Soundness: The main benchmarks do not convincingly test the claimed feasibility bottleneck. Every evaluated family has an immediate, analytically known feasible assignment: all zeros for IS, CA, and the stated NBI formulation, and all ones for MVC and SC. In particular, NBI is generated with positive A and b=Aξ+ε, so x=0 is feasible. Achieving 100% feasibility on these families therefore does not establish an ability to repair difficult or general ILPs; comparison with these trivial constructive baselines is missing.

The central theoretical claim is false as stated. Proposition 1 says that positive aggregate constraint reward and zero bound penalty for all t<T imply x_T is feasible. For the integer constraint x≥2, starting at x_0=0 and moving to x_1=1 gives positive constraint improvement and no bound violation but remains infeasible at T=1. The proof silently redefines T to be a sufficiently large threshold, assumes a uniform positive increment δ, and assumes improvement continues until that threshold. It neither guarantees that the learned policy satisfies these premises nor establishes feasibility under the reported 95.2% empirical adherence. Thus the claimed 'theoretical reward-feasibility alignment' is substantially overstated.

Evaluation protocol: RL-SPH is stopped when the baselines finish rather than under a clearly uniform budget in the main comparison, while solver presolving and branching are disabled. This produces an artificial comparison to isolated solver heuristics rather than realistic solver behavior. The paper should report matched wall-clock and hardware-aware budgets, default-solver baselines, and preprocessing costs consistently.

Metric handling is problematic. PG, PI, and FT are averaged only over instances on which a method succeeds, which can make low-feasibility methods look artificially strong. The PI definition also mixes a percentage-valued PG with a value of 1 when no incumbent exists, potentially penalizing infeasibility less than a poor feasible incumbent. Statistical tests, multiple training seeds, and uncertainty over model training are absent; the displayed deviations appear to cover instances only.

The 17-instance MIPLIB study is too small and its selection protocol is unspecified, so it cannot support broad generalization claims. It reports only instances on which feasibility was obtained, without a denominator or comparison against trivial/problem-aware starts, and RL-SPH is dramatically worse than RHF on examples such as scpk4 and bppc8-02. Cross-problem transfer between IS and MVC actually fails completely unless both problem families are included during training.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive configuration details: the manuscript links component and baseline repositories but does not identify a released RL-SPH implementation, exact generated datasets, trained checkpoints, complete random seeds, or repeated-training protocol. Important implementation details are unclear, including how the structural vector whose dimension depends on the number of constraints is handled across differently sized MIPLIB instances and joint training.

Significance/originality: Learned local rewriting for combinatorial optimization and reward-shaped feasibility repair are reasonable extensions of established ideas, but the evidence does not substantiate the paper's broad claims of a general standalone ILP feasibility method or of resolving a critical open gap. The strongest supported conclusion is narrower: on several highly structured, same-distribution families with trivial feasible points, the policy can improve solution quality faster than selected isolated heuristics.

Limitations and ethics: Relevant computational limitations are discussed, but the manuscript does not foreground the most consequential limitation—the restricted and trivially feasible benchmark structure—and instead repeatedly generalizes to 'general ILPs' and a 'unified solver.' The generic assertion that no societal consequences need highlighting is also less useful than a brief discussion of deployment validation, feasibility checking, and application-dependent risks.

strengths: Originality/significance: RL-SPH is a useful learned start-primal-heuristic framework that repairs infeasible assignments without delegating feasibility to a complete ILP solver. Combining feasibility-aware variable selection, two-phase rewards, and a Transformer policy is a meaningful contribution, particularly for non-binary variables.

Soundness: The empirical study is unusually broad, covering five benchmark families with 100 test instances each, classical and learned baselines, ablations, distribution/size/density shifts, 17 MIPLIB cases, and integration with SCIP and Gurobi. RL-SPH consistently attains 100% empirical feasibility and often substantially improves solution quality or primal integral over the fully feasible classical baseline.

The ablations provide useful evidence for the method's components: feasibility-aware selection is much faster than uniform selection and is essential on CA, while the Transformer encoder is essential for feasibility on CA and markedly improves IS performance.

Presentation: The paper is polished and easy to follow. The algorithm, rewards, initialization procedures, dataset sizes, hyperparameters, hardware, and many implementation details are documented, and the appendix contains valuable sensitivity and qualitative analyses.

Limitations are discussed constructively, including quadratic variable-selection cost, extreme-scale bottlenecks, weak performance on some MIPLIB instances and constraint classes, and limited cross-problem transfer. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the methodological contribution.
weaknesses: The claimed theoretical reward-feasibility alignment is much weaker than advertised. Proposition 1 assumes that constraint violation strictly improves and bounds are satisfied at every pre-feasibility step—the behavior that must effectively be established—and then proves that persistent monotone progress eventually reaches feasibility. It neither shows that maximizing the proposed reward enforces these assumptions nor provides a feasibility guarantee for the learned policy. The reported 88.4–99.1% adherence confirms that the assumptions do not always hold.

The primal-integral definition appears internally inconsistent: PG is defined as a percentage through multiplication by 100, but a missing incumbent is assigned PG=1. Thus one second without any feasible solution can be penalized less than one second with a poor feasible solution. This can materially distort PI comparisons, especially for methods with long first-feasible times. PG, PI, and FT are also averaged only over successful instances, requiring careful joint interpretation with FR.

The feasibility benchmarks are less challenging than the framing suggests. Standard IS, CA, and the proposed NBI family have the all-zero assignment as an obvious feasible solution; MVC and set covering likewise have obvious problem-specific feasible assignments. In particular, NBI uses nonnegative A and b with nonnegative variables, making zero trivially feasible, so 100% feasibility on this dataset provides limited evidence about difficult non-binary feasibility repair. Testing general ILPs with mixed-sign coefficients, finite nontrivial bounds, equality constraints, and narrow or disconnected feasible regions would strengthen the central claim.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. Learned baselines are run largely with released default configurations on substantially different instance sizes, despite the authors noting their need for dataset-specific tuning. Classical heuristics and RL-SPH also use different computational resources, and RL-SPH's stopping time in the first experiment is tied to completion of all baselines rather than a clearly uniform budget. The 17 MIPLIB instances lack a stated selection protocol, leaving possible selection bias.

Reproducibility is adequate but incomplete. The manuscript does not provide an RL-SPH code release, exact experimental seeds, training-seed variance, or statistical-test details; the meaning of the reported ± values is unspecified. It is also unclear how variable-length constraint vectors in the structural and reward-context projections are batched or processed across instances with different numbers of constraints, which is particularly important for the claimed MIPLIB and cross-size generalization.

The evaluation appears to use a single trained model per setting, so uncertainty across stochastic RL training runs is not measured. The attention-map case study from one sample is also insufficient evidence that long-range dependency modeling explains the gains.

The impact statement is boilerplate and dismisses potential consequences. Although the work poses no evident acute ethical risk, a generic optimization method can affect allocation, logistics, and other consequential decisions; a brief discussion of downstream misuse, biased objectives or constraints, and computational cost would be more appropriate.
